source: Chan & Schunn (2015) The importance of iteration in creative conceptual combination
finding: Field data from OpenIDEO. Combining distant sources in one step did not raise the chance that an idea was shortlisted. The effect of distance was about zero.
numbers: 2,341 concepts, 4,557 inspirations, 12 problems, 1,190 contributors. Direct-distance subsample 456 concepts by 239 contributors. Adding direct distance to the controls model: chi2(1)=0.00, p=.92, AIC rose 335.57 to 337.57. Per-problem slopes: 6 positive, 6 negative (sign test p=1.00).
quote: direct effects of far combinations have a mean zero effect
limits: Observational, not randomised. Web platform where people post only ideas they like. Distance coded by automatic text similarity (coding correlated r=.39 to .48 with human coding).
agent_relevance: A far analogue by itself is a coin flip for quality. Do not treat a distant source as a quality boost; treat it as raw material that needs further work.

source: Chan & Schunn (2015) The importance of iteration in creative conceptual combination (indirect effects)
finding: Building on ideas that were themselves built from distant sources did help. Iteration turns a far combination into a creative one.
numbers: Indirect-distance subsample 522 concepts by 281 authors. Adding indirect distance: chi2(1)=3.26, p=.07 (marginal), AIC fell 384.65 to 383.39. A 0.10 rise in indirect distance = +0.45 log-odds of shortlisting; Pr(shortlist) from 0.13 to 0.19 at the sample mean. Effect did not vary by problem (chi2(2)=0.26, p=.44).
limits: Only marginal significance; wide confidence interval. The authors say 2 to 4 iterations seemed enough but more may be needed when people filter less.
agent_relevance: Supports pairing O7 (map an analogue) with a revise loop: a far mapping should feed a second and third pass, not be used once.

source: Chan & Schunn (2015) The importance of iteration in creative conceptual combination (lab literature review)
finding: Lab work agrees that far combinations raise novelty but is mixed on quality. Two lab studies found lower quality for far combinations; one found no effect. Cited: Baughman & Mumford 1995, Mobley et al. 1992 (lower quality).
numbers: Two lab studies: lower quality. One lab study: no significant effect. Novelty gain from distance is described as robust across many lab studies (Wilkenfeld & Ward 2001; Mobley 1992; Wisniewski 1997; others).
limits: Second-hand summary inside the 2015 paper; the lab papers themselves were not opened by this agent.
agent_relevance: Matches SCHEMA O7 note: distant sources lower the average and raise the spread. Use far analogues for open mode and at impasses.

source: Chan & Schunn (2015) The importance of iteration in creative conceptual combination (mechanism)
finding: Why far pairs give novelty: people generate emergent attributes, through finding alignable conflicts by analogical mapping and causal reasoning, and think more abstractly about distant pairs.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Hampton 1997 (alignable conflicts), Kunda et al. 1990 (causal reasoning), Mumford et al. 1997 (abstraction with distant concepts).
limits: Mechanism is cited theory, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: The useful step is the mapping plus a reconciling inference, not the juxtaposition. An O7 operator should force an explicit conflict list and a repair.

source: Gu, Wang, Zhang, Li (2025) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity (arXiv 2412.14141 v2)
finding: A prompted pipeline retrieves concepts at several abstraction levels from the references of a paper, then decomposes and recombines them. It scored closer to the real paper's idea than a direct-generation baseline.
numbers: 87 OAG-Bench papers, 3 to 5 key references each, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20241022. SPECTER cosine similarity to the target paper. DR-Sim 0.85 vs 0.78, UP-Sim 0.83 vs 0.75, KM-Sim 0.87 vs 0.77. Abstract says 7 to 10 percent gain.
limits: Weak evidence. Similarity to a published idea is not creativity. No human raters, no significance test, no variance, one run. No ablation of retrieval versus decomposition (no ablation section found). The key references are the true ingredients, so this is rediscovery, not distant search. Abstract's 7 to 10 percent does not match the key-mechanism gain (about 13 percent relative).
agent_relevance: Shows an ingredient list plus decompose-then-recombine can recover known ideas. It does not show that distant retrieval adds value. Do not cite it as support for far analogy.

source: Gu, Wang, Zhang, Li (2025) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity (arXiv 2412.14141 v2) (design)
finding: Each past idea is stored with a problem statement and three generalisation levels (L1 to L3); retrieval runs level by level through embeddings and a similarity filter, then an analyse step splits ideas into components and an integrate step rebuilds them.
numbers: Structured fields: problem structure, design rationale, universal principle, key mechanism. Four SPECTER similarity fields.
limits: Design description only. Value of the abstraction levels is not isolated experimentally.
agent_relevance: Stating a problem at a higher abstraction before retrieval is a cheap way to make cross-domain mapping possible; test it against a flat retrieval ourselves.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? (arXiv 2409.04109)
finding: Blind expert review: LLM research ideas were rated more novel than ideas by human experts, but not better overall. The agent also lacked diversity.
numbers: N=49 experts wrote ideas, N=79 reviewed, 298 reviews. Novelty: human 4.84 (n=119), AI 5.64 (n=109, p<.01 adjusted), AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p<.001). Overall: human 4.68, AI 4.85 (n.s.), AI rerank 5.34 (p=.04).
quote: AI ideas are judged as significantly more novel than human ideas (p < 0.05)
limits: Ideas were not executed; review is subjective (inter-reviewer agreement only 56.1 percent). Retrieval-augmented generation, not a pure combination test.
agent_relevance: Novelty is easy to get from LLMs; the bottleneck is selection and diversity. Fits G8: do not let the generator pick its own best idea.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? (arXiv 2409.04109) (diversity)
finding: Scaling up generation hits a ceiling of duplicates: most sampled ideas repeat earlier ones.
numbers: 4,000 seed ideas generated; duplicate = cosine above 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2); only about 200 non-duplicate ideas, about 5 percent.
limits: Threshold 0.8 chosen by manual inspection; one topic set.
agent_relevance: Many draws do not mean many distinct ideas. A dedup step on combination output is needed before any selection.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? (arXiv 2409.04109) (LLM as judge)
finding: LLM judges of idea quality are close to or below the level of human reviewers and are not reliable.
numbers: Best LLM judge Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4 percent accuracy, GPT-4o 61.1, Claude-3-Opus 63.5; human inter-reviewer consistency 56.1 percent. Authors conclude LLMs cannot yet evaluate ideas reliably.
limits: Small ground-truth set (ICLR submissions); accuracy definition is balanced pairwise.
agent_relevance: Never rely on a model judge to pick the best combination. Use blind, length-normalised judging or code checks.

source: Radensky et al. (2026) Scideator: facet recombination and novelty evaluation (arXiv 2409.14634 v7)
finding: Splitting papers into purpose, mechanism and evaluation facets and recombining them by analogy gave researchers more creativity support than the same LLM without facets.
numbers: 22 CS researchers (16 PhD), 20-minute sessions each, within-subject. Creativity Support Index median 70.5 vs 61.0 (Wilcoxon p<.01). Gains in exploration and expressiveness; no difference in immersion.
limits: Self-reported support, not blind quality of ideas. Small N, researchers' own tool use.
agent_relevance: A typed facet split (purpose vs mechanism) is the human-validated way to set up an analogue mapping. Maps onto O7's typed mapping.

source: Radensky et al. (2026) Scideator (distance use)
finding: Participants used input and near facets far more than far facets. Main reason for skipping far facets: low perceived relevance. Four found far facets useful for discovery.
numbers: Same 22-participant study. Figure 3b shows near and input facets chosen substantially more than far ones; participants more often picked their own facets than let the LLM choose.
limits: Counts are shown in a figure; exact values not read. Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Humans filter out far analogues by relevance. An agent that does the same will rarely use them. Far sources need an explicit forcing step.

source: Radensky et al. (2026) Scideator (novelty checker ablation)
finding: Facet-based retrieval and re-ranking found overlapping prior work far better than ordinary retrieval, and a facet-grounded novelty classifier beat zero-shot.
numbers: Retrieval of known overlapping papers, complete system 89.66 percent vs 13.79 (relevance re-rank), 10.34 (embedding filter), 8.62 (snippet), 5.17 (keyword). Classifier on 43 held-out ideas (26 novel, 17 not): zero-shot accuracy 0.68, macro F1 0.65; AI Scientist prompt 0.47 / 0.44.
limits: Small test set (43). The facet-grounded classifier numbers were not all extracted. Retrieval test only on 'not novel' items. The table row labels were read from a flattened layout, so the mapping of 13.79, 10.34, 8.62, 5.17 to variants follows the listed order.
agent_relevance: Combination output needs a novelty check against prior art; checking by facet beats checking by whole idea.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji, Hope (2024) SciMON (arXiv 2305.14259 v7)
finding: Retrieving inspirations from past papers and iterating to push novelty works partly, but model ideas stay far below published ideas in depth and novelty.
numbers: Study II: ground-truth paper idea judged significantly higher in technical level and novelty in 85 percent of comparisons (rest ambiguous). Novelty iteration: first iteration gained novelty on 54 to 56 percent of ideas (GPT4FS +54.4, +SN +55.6); second iteration +57.8 percent. Study I: GPT4FS 73 percent rated helpful vs 33 for GPT3.5 few-shot.
limits: Six NLP expert raters; ratings from abstracts only. Authors note ideas are often superficial recombinations of common concepts.
agent_relevance: Iterative novelty pushing against retrieved prior art is a working loop but yields shallow recombination, matching Chan and Schunn: a single combination step is not enough.

source: Hope et al. (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining (arXiv 1706.05585)
finding: Retrieving products with the same purpose but different mechanism (far analogies) increased the share of good ideas in a crowd ideation task.
numbers: 38 AMT workers, 749 ideas, 5 grad-student judges (Fleiss kappa 0.51). Strict k=3: Pr(good) 0.56 vs TF-IDF 0.16 vs random 0.14. Lenient k=2: 0.71 vs 0.28 vs 0.27 (B about -1.9, p<.01). On the 9 shared seeds: 46 percent good (N=105) vs random 37 (49) vs TF-IDF 30 (54).
limits: Crowd workers, redesign task, wide confidence intervals (k=2 CI 0.48 to 0.87). Purpose-and-mechanism vectors were trained on 8,500 products. Random baseline sits above surface-similarity baseline, so near analogues may hurt (fixation).
agent_relevance: Best direct support that retrieving by purpose and then diversifying by mechanism helps. A structure-based analogue source beat surface similarity in humans.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (arXiv 2212.09196)
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat students on verbal and matrix analogies but was clearly worse on story analogies that need causal relations, especially across domains.
numbers: Story analogies (Gentner et al. materials), humans N=54: GPT-3 picked the causal match in near analogy (binomial p=.0039) but not far analogy (p=.065). Humans significant in both (far t(53)=16.7). Human advantage OR=0.37 (p=.0003); 15 of 54 humans were perfect.
limits: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003); GPT-4 tested only preliminarily and looked better. Multiple-choice, not generation.
agent_relevance: Far, causal mapping was the weak spot of the model that most resembles our backbone then. Check a mapping with code or an explicit relation list.

source: Choi et al. (2024) AnaloBench (arXiv 2402.12370, EMNLP 2024)
finding: Finding an analogous story gets much harder as stories get longer, and retrieving analogues from a large bank is near random for the best models.
numbers: 340 human-written analogies. Gap between humans and GPT-4: 6.9 points at 1 sentence, 28.8 points at 30 sentences. Random baseline 25 percent. Scale helps on short stories but little on long ones. Retrieval of top-k from the large bank: GPT-4-Turbo near trivial baseline for longer stories.
limits: Multiple-choice and retrieval format; stories extended by GPT-4 itself (checked with Claude: little change, section 5.1).
agent_relevance: Unaided analogue retrieval from memory over long, rich descriptions is weak. Supply a short abstracted statement of the problem structure first.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (arXiv 2310.01714, ICLR 2024)
finding: Asking the model to write its own relevant example problems before solving gave small to moderate gains over 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K 77.8 vs 5-shot CoT 76.7 vs 0-shot CoT 75.8; MATH 37.3 vs 34.9 vs 33.9 (PaLM2 MATH 34.8 vs 34.3). Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-4 19% vs 16 to 17% baselines. Far larger jumps for text-davinci-003 (GSM8K 61.0 vs 54.0), which used a demo prompt.
limits: Row mapping read from a flattened table; headline figures only. Self-generated analogues are near (same task type), not distant. Small effects on strong models.
agent_relevance: Self-generated near analogues are a cheap, small positive. They do not test distant combination.

source: Keshwani & Casakin (2024) Comparing analogy-based methods: bio-inspiration and engineering-domain inspiration (Biomimetics 9:344)
finding: Novice design teams chose biological (far) analogies most often. Biological analogies gave more novel designs than within-domain (near) ones, but not more than cross-domain engineering analogies.
numbers: 26 teams, 136 ideas selected. Selection share: biological 45.5 percent, cross-domain 29.4, within 25. Novelty pairwise (n bio=178, cross=123, within=78): bio vs within p=0.012; bio vs cross p=0.088; cross vs within p=0.084. Novelty share: 47, 32.4, 20.6 percent. Hypothesis cross > within > bio on selection was not supported.
limits: Novices; only novelty rated, no quality; small teams; designers may have found far biological analogies hard to apply.
agent_relevance: A middling distance may do as well as the farthest. Prefer a medium-distance source first and go farther only at impasses.

source: Xi, Cheng, Soni, Turner (2026) Evaluating creative generative AI with conceptual blending (ACL 2026 EvalEval position poster)
finding: Position paper: creativity in generative AI should be scored as integration of distinct frames with emergent structure, not as surface novelty. Proposes rubric: completeness, clarity, relevance, understanding depth, coherence, execution time.
numbers: No data in the poster. Names temperature tuning and style prompts as raising only surface novelty.
limits: Position paper with no experiments. Poster only; not a full paper.
agent_relevance: A usable blend checklist for an O7 verifier: both frames present, roles preserved, an emergent element in neither input, coherence.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Vibe Spaces for creatively connecting visual concepts (arXiv 2512.14884)
finding: Frontier LLM and image models tend to blend distant concepts by interpolating pixels, copying style or composing parts, not by merging the key shared attribute. A method that finds the shared attribute is preferred on hard pairs.
numbers: Ten human participants. Human preference for blends on one high-difficulty pair group: Ours 60.0 percent vs GPT 20.0, Gemini 6.67, CLIP-average 13.3. Human-human agreement 63 to 77 percent but Cohen kappa only 0.16 to 0.33. LLM judge top-1 agreement with humans 35.7 percent (chance 25).
limits: Visual domain, ten raters, low kappa. Read from a flattened table, so row alignment is partly uncertain.
agent_relevance: Fits the failure mode of juxtaposition without picking the right shared attribute. Name the shared attribute before blending.

source: Rethinking creativity evaluation: a critical analysis of existing creativity evaluations (arXiv 2508.05470)
finding: Common automatic creativity measures, including LLM judges, do not track idea-level creativity well.
numbers: Research-ideation contribution score: Pearson r between human reviewers and LLM judge only 0.159; best case 0.234 (GPT-4o, contribution). LLM judge unstable under small prompt changes. Creativity Index for human expert vs LLM creative writing 0.72 vs 0.53.
limits: Authors' own benchmark; scoring prompts vary; some domains' truth labels are proxies (accepted vs rejected papers).
agent_relevance: Another reason to avoid an LLM judge for open-mode idea ranking.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2026) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models (Sci Rep 16:3847)
finding: On a task of naming 10 words as unrelated as possible (a remote-association measure), GPT-4 beat the average of 100,000 humans, but the top 10 percent of humans beat every model tested.
numbers: 100,000 human DAT responses. GPT-4 above human mean; GeminiPro not different from humans; GPT-4-turbo worse than GPT-4. GPT-4 at highest temperature (1.5) scored 85.6, above 72 percent of humans. A strategy prompt using etymology beat the base DAT prompt for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. GPT-4 outputs repeated words (microscope in 70 percent of sets).
limits: Word-level semantic distance, not combination quality. Newer model versions did not always improve.
agent_relevance: Distance is easy to get from an LLM; use a strategy prompt and temperature for spread, and test for repeated words across draws.

source: Koch et al. (2025) Time-on-task and instructions help humans keep up with AI: replication and extension (Sci Rep 15:20173)
finding: Replication of the claim that chatbots out-create humans on the Alternate Uses Task. It mostly replicated, but the human deficit vanished on maximum scores when humans got better instructions and more time.
numbers: Original (Koivisto and Grassini): humans n=256, AI N=33. Here modified humans n=50; AI N=93 over four chatbots. AI mean scores higher in both conditions; AI maximum higher in original and in the Remote Associates Task; no significant human-AI difference on maximum score in the modified task.
limits: Task is divergent use generation and a remote associates task, not combination of concepts. Snapshot of chatbots in 2023 to 2024. Rating agreement for the nonsense check kappa 0.39.
agent_relevance: Many human-versus-AI creativity gaps depend on instructions and time. Compare like with like (same time budget, quality plus quantity instruction).

source: Baughman & Mumford (1995) and Mobley, Doares, Mumford (1992), as cited by Chan & Schunn 2015
finding: Lab studies of conceptual combination found that more distant combined concepts gave more novel but lower-quality products.
numbers: Not read by this agent; Chan and Schunn only state that both found lower quality for more distant combinations.
limits: Second-hand through one review. Do not quote effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Treat 'novelty up, quality down' as the lab baseline, to be rechecked before use.

source: Wilkenfeld & Ward (2001) Similarity and emergence in conceptual combination, as cited by Chan & Schunn 2015
finding: Lab work cited as showing that more dissimilar pairs produce more novel combined concepts.
numbers: Not read by this agent; no numbers.
limits: Second-hand; only the citation in Chan and Schunn was seen.
agent_relevance: Emergent attributes are the measurable product of a good combination; a verifier can ask for them.

source: Koivisto & Grassini (2023) human vs chatbot Alternate Uses Task, as described by Koch et al. 2025
finding: Original finding that chatbots had higher originality on the Alternate Uses Task than students.
numbers: Per Koch et al.: humans n=256, AI N=33 (three chatbots, 11 sessions each); 30 s per item for humans.
limits: Second-hand through the replication paper.
agent_relevance: The replication above is the better-powered check of this claim.

source: Gentner et al. story-analogy materials (Experiment 2), as used by Webb et al. 2023
finding: Humans rate stories sharing causal relations as more similar; the near (literal vs mere appearance) and far (true vs false analogy) comparisons both separate on causal structure.
numbers: Per Webb et al.: near and far conditions each had a correct and an incorrect target; GPT-3 failed to be reliable on far.
limits: Second-hand; the original paper was not opened; year approximate.
agent_relevance: Confirms that structure, not surface, is the criterion that separates a true analogue from a false one.

source: Gu et al. 2025 versus Chan & Schunn 2015 (synthesis of opened sources)
finding: Comparing what holds up: human field data show distance alone is zero-effect and iteration is what pays; the LLM paper reports gains in similarity to known ideas without measuring creativity.
numbers: Human: chi2(1)=0.00, p=.92 for direct distance; +0.45 log-odds per 0.10 indirect distance (p=.07). LLM: 0.85 vs 0.78 similarity, no test, N=87.
limits: Different outcomes (shortlist vs SPECTER similarity), so no direct comparison of effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Design the O7 step as map, then critique and rebuild at least twice, and measure with blind diverse raters, not similarity to a target.
